ACUTE ABDOMEN & SURGICAL PRINCIPLES__Acu:
Overview — The Decisive Fork: Upper vs Lower

The fork that governs the entire workup = upper vs lower, divided by the ligament of Treitz:

Upper GI Bleed

Oesophagus, stomach or duodenum (proximal to the ligament of Treitz). → triaged to endoscopy (OGD).

Lower GI Bleed

Below the ligament of Treitz. → triaged to imaging / colonoscopy.

SAFETY RULE: a haemodynamically unstable patient with a large fresh PR bleed has an upper GI bleed until proven otherwise (a brisk upper bleed transits fast and presents as fresh rectal blood).
VOCABULARY: haematemesis / “coffee-ground” vomit + melaena → upper; haematochezia (fresh PR blood) → usually lower.

Cross-ref: cirrhosis / varices (the variceal cause), peptic ulcer, diverticular disease, angiodysplasia, shock (resuscitation).

Two Universal First Principles (before you localise)
Resuscitate First (A–E)

Unstable bleeds need urgent resuscitation, wide-bore IV access and blood products until stable; activate the major haemorrhage protocol; correct coagulopathy. Use a restrictive transfusion strategy — transfuse red cells for Hb <70 g/L (target 70–90 g/L) unless there is massive haemorrhage or haemodynamic instability (NICE).

The FBC Trap

Acute bleeds may NOT initially show anaemia — Hb concentration lags (takes time to haemodilute), so a normal Hb never reassures in an acute bleed.

Angiodysplasia (high-yield vascular cause)
Angiodysplasia
  • The most common vascular abnormality of the GI tract; AVMs forming most often in the caecum and ascending colon; 2nd commonest cause of rectal bleeding in over-60s and commonest cause of small-bowel bleeding.
  • Presents as painless occult / recurrent PR bleeding; stops spontaneously in >90% but often recurs.
  • Associations: aortic stenosis (Heyde's syndrome), chronic renal failure, von Willebrand disease.
  • Managed with argon plasma coagulation (APC); capsule endoscopy preferred for small-bowel lesions.
📷 Image placeholder — angiodysplasia at colonoscopy — a flat, bright-red spider-like or fern-like cluster of ectatic mucosal vessels in the caecum/ascending colon, treated with argon plasma coagulation
Clinical Features & Assessment
  • Haematochezia (fresh / maroon PR blood); painless suggests diverticular / angiodysplasia, painful suggests colitis / ischaemia.
  • All patients need a DRE + proctoscopy (exclude a bedside-treatable anorectal source — haemorrhoids).
  • Risk factors for adverse outcome: haemodynamic instability, ongoing haematochezia, age >60, creatinine >150, significant comorbidities.
  • Oakland score: stratifies whether outpatient management is feasible (age, sex, previous LGIB admissions, PR findings, HR, SBP, Hb).
Investigations — the stability-driven imaging fork

Bloods: FBC, U&Es, LFT, clotting and Group & Save as a minimum; stool cultures to exclude infective causes.

Stable (~80%)

Mild & self-limiting → colonoscopy once stable + bowel-prepped (diagnostic + therapeutic).

Unstable

Resuscitate + correct coagulopathy + major haemorrhage protocol, then urgent CT angiogram BEFORE any endoscopic therapy → permits IR embolisation.

📷 Image placeholder — CT mesenteric angiography of active GI bleeding — a blush of contrast extravasating into the bowel lumen, localising the bleeding point to guide interventional-radiology embolisation
If colonoscopy is negative: do an OGD to look for an upper source; if still inconclusive → capsule endoscopy or RBC scintigraphy.
Management
~80% settle spontaneously — stable, low-risk young patients in whom bleeding has stopped can be discharged for outpatient investigation.
  • Endoscopic therapy (clips, thermal, APC for angiodysplasia, band ligation).
  • IR embolisation (via CT angiogram) for ongoing bleeding not controlled endoscopically.
  • Surgery = last resort (unstable despite resuscitation, or failed endoscopic / IR control).

Overview

Inflammation of the appendix — a blind-ended tube from the caecum where the three taeniae coli converge. Peak age teens–20s (second decade); children are the can't-miss high-risk group (atypical presentation + high perforation risk).

The decisive cascade: Luminal obstruction → trapped secretions → infection & inflammation → gangrene → rupture → peritonitis. The timeline drives urgency.
Causes of luminal obstruction
  • Faecolith — compacted faecal stone (classic)
  • Lymphoid hyperplasia — commoner in younger patients (post-viral)
  • Undigested seeds / impacted stool
  • Caecal tumour — the can't-miss cause in older patients
Cross-references
  • Acute abdomen (RIF pain workup)
  • Meckel's diverticulum (found at operation if appendix normal)
  • Mesenteric adenitis (paediatric mimic)
  • Gynae / urological RIF differentials
Clinical Features
📷 Image placeholder — McBurney's point — two-thirds of the way along a line from the umbilicus to the right anterior superior iliac spine, the surface marking of maximal tenderness in appendicitis
Cardinal pain pattern: Starts central / peri-umbilical (dull, poorly localised — visceral midgut pain) → migrates to RIF (sharp, well localised — parietal peritoneal inflammation). Worse on coughing / speed bumps.
Symptoms
  • Pain — central → RIF migration (key feature)
  • Vomiting after pain (pain-first = appendicitis order; vomiting-first = gastroenteritis)
  • Anorexia, nausea
  • Constipation > diarrhoea; pelvic appendicitis → rectal irritation / loose stool
Examination findings
  • McBurney's point tenderness
  • Rebound + percussion tenderness + guarding → peritonism
  • RIF mass → appendiceal abscess
  • Sepsis signs in severe cases (tachycardia, hypotension)
  • Rovsing's sign — LIF palpation → RIF pain
  • Psoas sign — RIF pain on right hip extension → retrocaecal appendix
Children — atypical & high-risk: Often present with diarrhoea, urinary symptoms, or left-sided pain. Examine GI, urinary AND genitals in all boys (exclude testicular torsion). Child <6 years with symptoms >48 hours = high perforation risk → active observation.
Differentials
Adults (RIF pain)
  • Gynaecological — ovarian cyst rupture, ectopic pregnancy, PID
  • Renal — ureteric colic, UTI, pyelonephritis
  • GI — Crohn's, Meckel's diverticulum, diverticular disease
  • Urological — testicular torsion, epididymo-orchitis
Paediatric differentials
  • Mesenteric adenitis — inflamed mesenteric nodes, often post-URTI/tonsillitis; commonest paediatric mimic
  • Gastroenteritis, constipation
  • Intussusception, UTI
  • Testicular torsion (boys)
💡 Normal appendix at operation? Inspect the distal ileum for an inflamed Meckel's diverticulum — a congenital blind-ended diverticulum ~60 cm from the ileocaecal valve that can inflame, rupture, or cause volvulus/intussusception.
Investigations
📷 Image placeholder — CT of acute appendicitis — a dilated, thick-walled, fluid-filled appendix (>6 mm) with surrounding fat stranding, sometimes containing an appendicolith
Appendicitis is a clinical diagnosis. Raised inflammatory markers + clinical findings = sufficient to warrant appendicectomy. Imaging only if features are inconclusive.
Alvarado score (MANTRELS, /10): a clinical scoring aid — Migration of pain, Anorexia, Nausea/vomiting, Tenderness RIF (2), Rebound, Elevated temperature, Leucocytosis (2), Shift (neutrophilia). ≥7 supports appendicitis; ≤3 makes it unlikely. Supports — not replaces — clinical judgement.
🩸
FBC + CRP + G&S
Neutrophil-predominant leucocytosis; ↑ CRP. G&S if surgical intervention planned.
🔬
Urine dip + pregnancy test
Urinalysis to exclude renal/urological causes. Serum hCG (pregnancy test) mandatory in all reproductive-age women — exclude ectopic.
📷
USS / CT (if equivocal)
USS first if gynaecological differentials (esp. transvaginal USS). USS preferred over CT in children (avoid radiation). CT if diagnosis remains unclear.
Management
Surgical (gold standard)
  • Laparoscopic appendicectomy — gold standard; inspect whole abdomen for other pathology
  • Pregnancy — laparoscopic appendicectomy is now considered safe in all trimesters (RCOG) and is increasingly preferred; an open/muscle-splitting (Lanz) approach remains an alternative, especially in advanced pregnancy
  • Prophylactic IV antibiotics peri-operatively → reduce SSI
  • Appendix sent for routine histopathology (exclude malignancy)
  • Drain any abscess before appendicectomy
Special scenarios
  • Appendiceal mass — IV antibiotics + interval appendicectomy 6–8 weeks later
  • Pelvic abscess — fever + RIF mass; confirmed on CT; managed with antibiotics + percutaneous drainage
  • Antibiotic-only management — growing evidence base for selected uncomplicated adults; surgery remains gold standard but increasingly examined alternative
Complications
Perforation
  • Peritoneal contamination → generalised peritonitis
  • Especially in children with delayed presentation (>48 h)
  • Signs: sudden pain relief then worsening, rigid abdomen, sepsis
Other complications
  • Appendiceal mass — omentum + small bowel wall off the appendix
  • Pelvic abscess — fever + palpable RIF mass; CT-confirmed; IV abx + percutaneous drainage
  • Surgical site infection
  • Stump appendicitis (rare — if insufficient appendix removed)

Overview

Pre-operative assessment = identify comorbidities that risk complications during anaesthesia, surgery, or recovery. Timing: 2–4 weeks before surgery (leaves time to optimise).

Urgency dictates depth: Elective surgery → delay and optimise (e.g. poorly controlled diabetes). Emergency surgery → proceed with whatever optimisation time allows.

Overview — Goals of Pre-operative Management
Pre-operative management optimises the patient's condition before surgery to minimise perioperative risk. It translates findings from pre-operative assessment into action. Key domains: consent, fasting, medication management, DVT prophylaxis, bowel prep, skin prep, and same-day checks.
Consent
Valid consent requires (MCA 2005)
  • Capacity: understand, retain, weigh, communicate decision
  • Voluntary: free from coercion
  • Informed: material risks, benefits, alternatives explained
  • Written consent (form 1/3) for procedures under GA or significant risk
  • Surgeon or trainee supervised by surgeon should obtain consent
Montgomery ruling (2015)
  • Patient must be told of ALL material risks — those a reasonable patient would want to know, or that this specific patient would consider significant
  • Replaces the old Bolam standard for consent
  • Surgeon must tailor risk discussion to the individual
  • Document the discussion, not just the signature
Capacity lacking: Act in best interests (MCA). For elective surgery, delay until capacity returns if possible. For emergency, proceed in best interests — consult next of kin (advisory, not legally binding) + document + consider IMCA.

VTE Prophylaxis
All surgical patients must have VTE risk assessment (NICE NG89). DVT + PE = leading cause of preventable hospital death.
Mechanical prophylaxis (all surgical patients)
  • TED stockings (thigh-length) — all patients
  • Intermittent pneumatic compression (IPC) — intra-op + post-op until mobile; especially orthopaedic, major abdominal surgery
  • Early mobilisation
  • Adequate hydration
Pharmacological prophylaxis (LMWH)
  • Start: 6–12 h post-op (once haemostasis confirmed)
  • Duration: 7–10 days standard; 28 days for major abdominal/pelvic cancer surgery
  • Withhold if: epidural in-situ (wait 12 h after removal), active bleeding, platelets <50
  • Renal dose adjustment if eGFR <30 (use unfractionated heparin)
Caprini / local trust VTE risk tools stratify patients. High-risk factors: malignancy, previous VTE, thrombophilia, immobility, BMI >30, major pelvic/lower limb surgery.
Diabetes Management Perioperatively
General principles
  • Schedule first on the morning list where possible — minimises fasting time
  • Target BM 6–10 mmol/L perioperatively (avoid hypoglycaemia and hyperglycaemia)
  • Check BM 2-hourly whilst NBM
  • Involve diabetic specialist nurse / endocrine team
VRIII (Variable Rate Insulin Infusion)
  • Indicated: T1DM; T2DM on insulin; major surgery; BM uncontrolled pre-op
  • Run alongside 5% glucose + 0.45% NaCl + 0.15% KCl
  • Avoid plain 0.9% saline — causes hyperchloraemic acidosis
  • Monitor BM hourly on VRIII; electrolytes 4–6 hourly
  • Convert back to S/C insulin at first meal
Bowel Preparation & Skin Prep
Bowel prep
  • Routine mechanical bowel prep NOT recommended for most colorectal surgery (ERAS / NICE evidence: no mortality/anastomotic leak benefit, causes dehydration)
  • Still used for: left colonic anastomoses (some centres), rectal surgery, laparoscopic colectomy with intra-op colonoscopy
  • Oral antibiotics (erythromycin + neomycin) ± IV antibiotics at induction for colorectal cases
Skin prep & SSI prevention
  • Chlorhexidine 2% in 70% alcohol — superior to povidone-iodine for SSI prevention (NICE NG125)
  • Prophylactic antibiotics at induction (not before, not >30 min after)
  • Hair removal: clippers NOT razor (razors cause micro-abrasions → ↑SSI)
  • Maintain normothermia (warm air blanket, warm IV fluids)
  • Maintain normoglycaemia (↑glucose → ↑SSI risk)
ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery)
Multimodal protocol across pre-, intra-, and post-operative phases. Reduces complications, length of stay, and costs. Now standard for colorectal, orthopaedic, and major abdominal surgery.
Pre-operative ERAS elements
  • Patient education and goal-setting
  • Prehabilitation (exercise, nutrition, smoking cessation)
  • Carbohydrate loading (as above)
  • Avoid prolonged fasting / bowel prep

Overview — The Three R's

Every fluid prescription begins with identifying which of the Three R's applies.

NICE (CG174) frames this as the 5 Rs: Resuscitation, Routine maintenance, Replacement, Redistribution (e.g. third-spacing) and Reassessment — the three R's below plus redistribution and continuous reassessment.
Resuscitation
  • Patient is in shock / hypovolaemia
  • Rapid isotonic bolus to restore perfusion
Replacement
  • Patient has ongoing abnormal losses (vomiting, NG, stoma, diarrhoea)
  • Maintenance ± adjustments for deficits and losses
Maintenance
  • Patient is NBM but euvolaemic — just covering daily requirements
  • 25–30 mL/kg water + 1 mmol/kg Na/K/Cl + 50–100 g glucose
Fluid Compartments & Tonicity
📷 Image placeholder — body fluid compartments — total body water split into intracellular (⅔) and extracellular (⅓), with the extracellular fluid further divided into interstitial (~80%) and intravascular/plasma (~20%)
Body water distribution
  • Intracellular = ⅔ of total body water
  • Extracellular = ⅓ — split into intravascular (20%) and interstitial (80%)
  • Third space = peritoneal, pleural, pericardial cavities (don't normally hold fluid)
  • Third-spacing = fluid shifts out of vessels into these spaces → hypovolaemia + oedema simultaneously
Tonicity
  • Normal serum osmolality: 275–295 mOsmol/kg
  • Isotonic (saline, Hartmann's) → stays extracellular → best for resus
  • Hypotonic (5% dextrose, 0.18% saline) → water moves into cells → maintenance only; hyponatraemia risk if overused
  • Hypertonic (3% saline) → pulls water out of cells

Get senior help if the patient is shocked or not responding. Establish the cause (sepsis, haemorrhage, etc.) alongside resuscitation.

  • Fluid: 0.9% saline, Hartmann's, or Plasma-Lyte 148 (isotonic)

  • Repeat 250–500 mL boluses as needed
  • Seek expert help after ~2000 mL if not responding
K⁺ safety rule
  • K⁺ infusion rate must never exceed 10 mmol/hr

Anaphylactic Shock

IgE-mediated (Type I hypersensitivity) → massive mast cell degranulation → histamine, tryptase → ↓SVR + bronchospasm + ↑vascular permeability. Triggers: drugs (penicillin, NSAIDs), foods (nuts), latex, stings.
Clinical features
Presentation
  • Skin: urticaria, erythema, angioedema (lips, tongue, throat)
  • Airway: stridor, hoarseness (laryngeal oedema)

Management (Resus Council 2021)
  • Remove trigger
  • IM adrenaline 0.5 mg (0.5 mL of 1:1000) into anterolateral thigh — FIRST
  • Repeat at 5 min if no improvement

  • IV fluid bolus 500 mL – 1 L crystalloid
  • Antihistamine — no longer part of initial emergency care; a non-sedating oral antihistamine (e.g. cetirizine) may be given after stabilisation for persistent skin symptoms (RCUK 2021)

  • ECG: STEMI, new LBBB
  • Echo: confirms low EF, wall motion abnormality
  • Troponin ↑, BNP ↑
Management
  • Revascularisation ASAP — primary PCI if MI; this is the definitive treatment
  • Vasopressors: noradrenaline (MAP ≥65) ± dobutamine (inotrope)
  • Avoid fluids if pulmonary oedema present
  • Furosemide if fluid overloaded
  • IABP / impella (mechanical circulatory support) in refractory cases
  • ICU admission

Overview

A hernia is an organ or its fascia protruding outside the walls of its usual cavity. Inguinal hernias account for 75% of all abdominal hernias.

The two decisive forks
  • Is it complicated? Reducible & wide-necked → safe-ish. Irreducible / narrow-necked → incarceration → obstruction → strangulation
  • Which anatomical type? Each defined by where it emerges

  • Bowel obstruction — hernia is a top-3 cause
  • GORD — hiatus hernia
  • Stomas — parastomal hernia
Presentation & Examination
Typical presentation
  • Soft lump through abdominal wall
  • Reducible — pushes back on lying down or gentle pressure
  • Protrudes on coughing (↑ intra-abdominal pressure) or standing (gravity)
  • Aching / dragging sensation
Examining a groin lump — structured check
  • Cough impulse (irreducible hernia may lose this)
  • Location relative to pubic tubercle — the key discriminator
  • Reducible on lying down / gentle pressure?
  • If entering scrotum — can you get above it / separate from testis?
The single highest-yield discriminator: Inguinal = superomedial to the pubic tubercle. Femoral = inferolateral to the pubic tubercle.

Management: resuscitate (large-bore IV ×2, bloods, cross-match, IV fluids/blood), identify bleeding source, urgent surgical review. Secondary haemorrhage = infection control + surgical re-exploration.
Respiratory Complications
Atelectasis (Day 0–2 — commonest early fever)
  • Collapse of lung segments due to under-ventilation (pain → shallow breathing → mucous plugging)
  • Presents: fever, ↑RR, ↓SpO₂, reduced air entry at bases
  • CXR: basal shadowing
  • Management: adequate analgesia (allows deep breathing), chest physiotherapy, mobilisation, incentive spirometry
Pneumonia
  • Hospital-acquired (HAP) — gram-negative organisms common
  • Presents: fever, productive cough, ↑WCC, consolidation on CXR
  • Management: sputum culture, antibiotics per local protocol, O₂, physio
  • Risk ↑ with: prolonged ventilation, aspiration (dysphagia, NGT), immunosuppression
The analgesia link: adequate pain relief allows deep breathing and mobilisation → reduces atelectasis → reduces pneumonia. Under-treated pain → shallow breathing → retained secretions → infection.
Cardiovascular & Thromboembolic Complications
VTE — DVT & PE (Day 4–6)
  • DVT: unilateral leg swelling, pain, warmth, erythema
  • PE: pleuritic chest pain, dyspnoea, haemoptysis, ↑HR, hypoxia; massive PE → haemodynamic collapse
  • Investigations: D-dimer, Doppler USS (DVT), CTPA (PE)
  • Prevention: LMWH + TED stockings + early mobilisation; 28 days for major cancer surgery
  • Treatment: therapeutic LMWH → DOAC
Cardiac complications
  • Arrhythmias — especially new AF (surgery triggers sympathetic activation + hypoxia + electrolyte disturbance)
  • ACS / MI — surgical stress unmasks coronary disease; peak 2–3 days post-op; troponin + ECG
  • Stroke — embolic (AF, air embolus) or haemorrhagic (hypertension post-op)
  • Risk ↑ in: pre-existing cardiac disease, major vascular surgery, emergency operations
Gastrointestinal Complications
📷 Image placeholder — abdominal X-ray of post-operative ileus — gas-filled dilated loops of bowel throughout both small and large bowel (uniform dilatation), in contrast to mechanical obstruction where distended proximal loops give way to a collapsed distal bowel
Post-operative ileus
  • Functional bowel dysmotility — not mechanical obstruction
  • Common after abdominal/pelvic surgery, long anaesthetics, opioids, electrolyte disturbance
  • Presents: abdominal distension, vomiting, absent bowel sounds, no flatus or stool
  • AXR: dilated loops throughout (vs obstruction — dilated proximal, decompressed distal)
  • Management: drip & suck (IV fluids + NGT), correct electrolytes especially K⁺, mobilise, avoid opioids if possible
Anastomotic leak (Day 5–7)
  • Breakdown of a bowel join → GI contents into peritoneum
  • Presents: increasing pain, fever, peritonism, sepsis — can be subtle at first
  • Drain output becomes faeculent / turbid; CRP rises sharply on day 3–5
  • CT abdomen (with contrast) — confirms leak + free gas/fluid
  • Management: resuscitate, IV antibiotics, urgent re-operation (defunctioning stoma ± repair)
📷 Image placeholder — contrast CT of an anastomotic leak — extraluminal free gas and fluid collection adjacent to the bowel anastomosis, with contrast leaking from the lumen
Late GI complications
  • Adhesions → small bowel obstruction (most common cause of SBO in adults)
  • Incisional hernia → protrusion through the scar (esp. midline laparotomy); risk ↑ with: obesity, infection, poor nutrition, steroids
  • Constipation — opioids + immobility; prescribe laxatives with opioids routinely
Wound Complications
📷 Image placeholder — burst abdomen (wound dehiscence / evisceration) — full-thickness separation of a midline laparotomy wound with loops of bowel/omentum protruding through the skin; a surgical emergency preceded by serosanguineous "pink fluid" leak
Surgical site infection (Day 5–7)
  • Erythema, warmth, swelling, purulent discharge, wound pain ± systemic sepsis
  • Superficial: skin/subcutaneous tissue; deep: fascia/muscle; organ/space (e.g. intra-abdominal abscess)
  • Management: wound swab, open and drain superficial infections, antibiotics for systemic features
  • Prevention: chlorhexidine skin prep, prophylactic antibiotics at induction, normothermia, normoglycaemia
Wound dehiscence / Burst abdomen
  • Dehiscence: partial separation of wound edges
  • Burst abdomen (evisceration): full-thickness separation with bowel/omentum protruding through skin — surgical emergency
  • Warning sign: serosanguineous "pink fluid" draining from wound (day 5–10)
  • Management: cover bowel with moist sterile dressings, urgent return to theatre, mass closure with non-absorbable sutures
  • Risk ↑: obesity, malnutrition, infection, steroids, poor surgical technique, coughing
Urinary Complications
UTI (Day 3–5)
  • Catheter-associated UTI — most common nosocomial infection post-op
  • Dysuria, frequency, suprapubic pain, cloudy urine ± systemic sepsis
  • Investigations: urine dip, MSU + culture
  • Management: antibiotics per local protocol, remove catheter as soon as possible
Urinary retention & AKI
  • Retention: common post-op (opioids, spinal anaesthesia, pelvic surgery); ♂ > ♀ (BPH risk); trial without catheter (TWOC) needed
  • AKI: hypovolaemia, sepsis, nephrotoxic drugs (NSAIDs, gentamicin, contrast) → oliguria (<0.5 mL/kg/hr) → rising creatinine; monitor UO + U&Es; fluid challenge if hypovolaemic
Systemic Complications
Anaemia
  • Post-op FBC at 24–48 h; causes: intra-op blood loss, haemodilution, haemolysis
  • Hb <100 g/L → oral/IV iron
  • Hb <70–80 g/L → blood transfusion (lower threshold if symptomatic, cardiac/respiratory disease)
  • Jehovah's Witnesses: may refuse transfusion by valid advance directive — respect autonomy if capacity present; optimise pre-op, use cell salvage, minimise intra-op loss
Post-op nausea & vomiting (PONV)
  • Risk factors (Apfel score): female, non-smoker, prior PONV/motion sickness, post-op opioids (each = 1 point; score ≥3 = high risk)
  • Prophylaxis: ondansetron + dexamethasone at induction (± cyclizine) in high-risk; use TIVA (propofol) instead of volatile agents
  • Treatment: ondansetron 4 mg IV/IM, cyclizine 50 mg IV, metoclopramide 10 mg IV
Post-operative delirium
  • Acute fluctuating confusion — common in elderly/frail post-op
  • Reversible causes (PINCH ME): Pain, Infection, Nutrition, Constipation, Hydration, Medication, Environment
  • Exclude: hypoxia, sepsis, urinary retention, hypoglycaemia
  • Management: treat cause, reorient, avoid antipsychotics unless severe agitation; avoid benzodiazepines (worsen delirium)
Nutrition post-op
  • Enteral preferred (oral → NG/PEG → jejunostomy)
  • Early feeding (day of surgery in ERAS) reduces infective complications + ileus + LOS
  • TPN via central line only if GI tract completely unusable — hypertonic solution scleroses peripheral veins
  • Screen with MUST; dietitian if complex needs
Analgesia & Procedural Support
Analgesic ladder (multimodal)
  • Step 1: regular paracetamol 1 g QDS
  • Step 2: add NSAIDs (ibuprofen, diclofenac) — avoid in: asthma, renal impairment, cardiac disease, peptic ulcer disease
  • Step 3: add weak opioid (codeine, tramadol) or strong opioid (morphine, oxycodone)
  • Prescribe laxatives with all opioids (prevent ileus + constipation)
  • Regional techniques (epidural, nerve block) reduce systemic opioid requirements
Patient-controlled analgesia (PCA)
  • IV opioid on-demand with lockout interval
  • Only the patient presses the button — safety mechanism; staff/family must not press it
  • Have naloxone available (respiratory depression), antiemetic (PONV), atropine (bradycardia)
  • Review daily — wean when oral intake re-established
Lines, tubes & drains — remove early (ERAS principle)
  • Urinary catheter: remove when mobile + no urological indication → TWOC; retention risk in males
  • Drains: remove when output <30 mL/24 h (or per surgeon — drain removal timing is contested)
  • IV cannulae: re-site every 72–96 h; inspect daily for phlebitis
  • NGT: remove when GI function returns and oral intake adequate
  • Every device left in longer than needed ↑ infection risk and impairs mobilisation
⭐ Exam Pearls
5 Ws pyrexia timeline
Wind (0–2) → Water (3–5) → Walking (4–6) → Wound (5–7) → Wonder drugs/line (any time)

Day 0–2. Treat with analgesia + physio + mobilisation. Inadequate analgesia → shallow breathing → atelectasis → pneumonia.

Reactive = <24 h (slipped ligature). Secondary = 7–10 d (infection erodes vessel).

Dilated loops throughout on AXR. Drip & suck + correct K⁺. No surgery needed.

↑ pain + fever + peritonism + sepsis. CRP spikes day 3–5. CT confirms. Emergency re-operation.
Burst abdomen = emergency
Pink fluid from wound = warning sign. Cover bowel with moist dressings → theatre urgently.

Female + non-smoker + prior PONV + post-op opioids. ≥3 = high risk. Prophylaxis: ondansetron + dex.
NSAIDs: avoid in asthma, renal, cardiac, ulcers
Multimodal analgesia reduces opioid need — combine paracetamol + NSAID + opioid step-wise.
PCA: only patient presses
Have naloxone + antiemetic + atropine available. Never press for the patient.
Anaemia thresholds
Hb <100 → oral/IV iron. Hb <70–80 → transfuse. Respect Jehovah's Witness advance directive.
Delirium: PINCH ME
Pain, Infection, Nutrition, Constipation, Hydration, Medication, Environment. Treat cause first.
Remove everything early (ERAS)
Catheter, drain, NGT, cannula — each device left in longer than needed ↑ infection + impairs mobilisation.

Drug Details
Paracetamol
  • MOA: inhibits central prostaglandin synthesis (COX)
  • Safe in renal failure, pregnancy, elderly
  • Hepatotoxic in overdose (N-acetylcysteine antidote)
  • IV paracetamol: rapid onset, useful peri-operatively
NSAIDs
  • MOA: inhibit COX-1/2 → ↓prostaglandin synthesis
  • Contraindications: peptic ulcer disease, CKD (↓GFR), HF, asthma (aspirin-sensitive), pregnancy (3rd trimester), warfarin use
  • SE: GI ulceration (give PPI cover), fluid retention, AKI
Opioids
  • Morphine: oral (IR for breakthrough, MR for regular) or IV. Gold standard strong opioid.
  • SE: N&V, constipation (always prescribe laxatives), sedation, respiratory depression, urinary retention
  • Antidote: naloxone (opioid antagonist) 0.4mg IV/IM — reverses all effects
  • Fentanyl: patch or IV. Preferred in renal failure.
  • Tramadol: weak opioid + noradrenaline/serotonin reuptake inhibitor. Seizure risk.
Adjuvants
  • Neuropathic pain: amitriptyline, duloxetine, gabapentin, pregabalin
  • Bone pain: NSAIDs + bisphosphonates
  • Opioid-sparing: ketamine (NMDA antagonist), clonidine
  • Regional: nerve blocks, epidurals (opioid + local anaesthetic)
Local Anaesthetics

Block sodium channels → prevent nerve depolarisation. Duration: lidocaine 1–2h, bupivacaine 4–8h. Max doses are critical.

💊
Lidocaine
Max 3mg/kg plain · 7mg/kg with adrenaline. Fast onset, medium duration. Used for infiltration, nerve blocks, IV regional.
💊
Bupivacaine
Max 2mg/kg. Long-acting. Used for epidurals, spinals, nerve blocks. Most cardiotoxic.
LA Toxicity
Perioral tingling → tinnitus → seizures → cardiovascular collapse. Treat: intralipid 20% (lipid emulsion) IV + resuscitation.

WHO ladder: regular paracetamol ± NSAIDs → add weak opioid → add strong opioid. Always prescribe laxatives with opioids.
NSAIDs contraindicated in: CKD, peptic ulcer, HF, 3rd trimester pregnancy, aspirin-sensitive asthma.
Naloxone: reverses all opioid effects including analgesia — titrate carefully to avoid precipitating pain.
Morphine in renal failure: accumulation of active metabolite (morphine-6-glucuronide) → use fentanyl instead.
LA toxicity: lipid emulsion (intralipid 20%) is antidote — lipid sink for LA molecules.

Overview — "If the gut works, use it"

The decisive fork governing every nutritional decision: choose the least invasive route the gut can tolerate.

RouteUse whenRequires working gut?
Oral supportPatient can swallow safelyYes
Enteral (tube)Unsafe/inadequate oral intake but functional GI tractYes
Parenteral (IV)GI tract non-functional, inaccessible, or perforatedNo
Screening & Defining Malnutrition (NICE CG32)
Screen all inpatients on admission and outpatients at first appointment. Repeat weekly for inpatients. Tool = MUST (Malnutrition Universal Screening Tool).
Malnourished — any one of:
  • BMI <18.5
  • Unintentional weight loss >10% in 3–6 months
  • BMI <20 + weight loss >5% in 3–6 months
At risk — any of:
  • Eaten little/nothing for >5 days (or likely to for next 5+)
  • Poor absorption or high losses
  • Increased needs from catabolism
Daily targets (not severely ill, no refeeding risk)
  • Energy: 25–35 kcal/kg (lower if BMI >25)
  • Protein: 0.8–1.5 g/kg
  • Fluid: 30–35 mL/kg (+ extra for drains/fistulae)
  • Plus: electrolytes, minerals, micronutrients, fibre
  • Seriously ill / >5 days nil intake: start at ≤50% of target for first 1–2 days, then build up
Enteral Tube Feeding
Indication — both must hold: (1) inadequate or unsafe oral intake AND (2) functional, accessible GI tract.
RouteSiteUse whenKey points
NGStomach (nasal)Short-term (<4 weeks)Most common; allows bolus + hypertonic feeds; easily displaced
NJJejunum (nasal)Short-term + delayed gastric emptying / reflux riskReduces aspiration risk; post-pyloric placement can be difficult
PEGStomach (percutaneous)Long-term (≥4 weeks)Stroke, MND, Parkinson's, oesophageal cancer; placed endoscopically under antibiotic cover; usable 4 h after insertion
PEJ / jejunostomyJejunum (percutaneous)Long-term + high reflux/aspiration riskPermits early post-op feeding; more technically demanding
The 4-week rule: <4 weeks → NG. ≥4 weeks → consider PEG. The single most-tested route rule.
NG safety (NPSA): Confirm position after placement and before every use — aspirate pH ≤5.5 on pH paper. X-ray if pH equivocal. Misplaced NG into the lung is a Never Event.
Parenteral Nutrition
Access — duration drives the line
  • <14 days, no other central need → peripheral venous catheter (mind pH/tonicity)
  • <30 days → non-tunnelled central catheter
  • >30 days (long-term) → tunnelled subclavian line

TPN typically via central line — hypertonic solution scleroses peripheral veins.

PN complications
  • Line sepsis — the big one; daily catheter-site inspection
  • Thrombosis
  • Refeeding syndrome (see below)
  • Deranged LFTs / cholestasis
  • Electrolyte and glucose disturbance

Trophic feeding — keep minimal enteral feeding alongside PN where possible → maintains gut function, reduces cholestasis.

Refeeding Syndrome — High-Yield Complication
Mechanism: Carbohydrate load → insulin surge → rapid intracellular electrolyte shift → ↓ phosphate (cardinal), ↓ K⁺, ↓ Mg²⁺ + expanding ECF volume. Thiamine demand spikes. Consequences: cardiac/respiratory failure, arrhythmias, rhabdomyolysis, seizures, coma.
High-risk criteria (NICE)
One of these aloneOr two of these
BMI <16BMI <18.5

Prevention & management (NICE)
  • Start at max 10 kcal/kg/day (5 kcal/kg in extreme cases, BMI <14)
  • Build to full needs over 4–7 days
  • Thiamine 200–300 mg/day + vitamin B co strong — before and during the first 10 days
  • Replace K⁺, PO₄³⁻, Mg²⁺ as needed; do not pre-correct electrolytes before starting feeding
Enteral Feeding Complications & Monitoring
Enteral complications
  • Tube-related: NG — discomfort, sinusitis, erosions; bronchial misplacement (fatal if used); PEG — stoma infection, peritonitis, dislodgement
  • Blockage — flush with water before and after every use
  • Infection — discard feed sets every 24 h
  • Aspiration — nurse at ≥30° during and after feeding; post-pyloric tubes for flat patients
  • GI symptoms — bloating, diarrhoea, nausea; slow rate or switch to continuous feed
Monitoring
  • Bloods (daily until stable): U&Es, glucose, Mg, phosphate; LFTs/INR, calcium, albumin, CRP
  • Trace elements (Zn, Cu, Se) periodically on long-term PN
  • Clinical: weight, BMI, fluid balance, GI tolerance, tube/stoma site
  • NG: pH check before every feed
  • PN lines: daily site inspection for infection
Ethics & End of Life — CANH
Clinically assisted nutrition and hydration (CANH) is a medical treatment — not basic care. It can be withheld or withdrawn like any treatment, using the same consent framework. Capacity drives the decision: competent patient's refusal must be respected. If they lack capacity, decide in best interests (advance directives, MDT, family).
